summary:
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Its parliament and courts handle domestic affairs, while Danish legislation on marriage and on official identity documents has been adopted and applies in Greenland. A visitor's legal position on those questions follows the Danish framework as received here.

Same-sex relations carry no criminal penalty. Since 2010 Article 100 of the Criminal Code has prohibited speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other protected categories, and the Code provides penalty enhancement for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation. No prosecution under either provision is recorded in the available sources.

Same-sex marriage took effect on 1 April 2016, adopting Danish legislation that passed unanimously on two occasions after the first bill lapsed in Danish elections. It replaced the registered partnership (nalunaarsukkamik inooqatigiinneq) that had run from 1 July 1996, whose application was repealed the day the marriage law commenced. The bishop of the established church supported the change. Marriage is available to a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status.

Legal change of sex designation on official documents rests on self-determination. The law, passed in 2016 and brought into force by decree, requires no sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilization or medical diagnosis. Applicants must be over 18 and state that they want their documentation changed, then observe a six-month reflection period to confirm the request.

Greenlandic passports are issued with an X sex descriptor in addition to male and female.

The Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination was passed by the parliament in May 2024 and took effect on 1 July 2024. It prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics, among other characteristics. It creates an Equal Treatment Board to handle discrimination complaints and an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination.

Public expression is visible. The first pride parade was held in Nuuk on 15 May 2010 and drew about 1,000 people, and a modest march has continued since. Accounts from 2015 describe gay life as low-key, integrated and non-violent, with no reported anti-LGBT violence.
tangentialFactors:
The 1996 partnership law passed with virtually no debate, and the marriage bill that replaced it passed unanimously twice. Political contestation over these questions is not documented in the available sources.

The small, scattered population supports almost no dedicated gay scene. Some nightclubs and bars in Nuuk draw a mixed gay and straight crowd.
localsOnly:
LGBT Qaamaneq was founded in August 2014 as a national association for lesbians, gay, bisexual and transgender people. It works for political, cultural and social equality and is open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters.

The Human Rights Council of Greenland is state-funded and works closely with the Danish Institute for Human Rights to promote and protect human rights.
outOfScopeNotes:
No prosecution under Article 100 or under the hate-crime penalty enhancement appears in the available sources, so enforcement practice is not documented.

The 2024 anti-discrimination law took effect on 1 July 2024. No complaint outcomes or decisions by the Equal Treatment Board are recorded.

The sources do not record how the X passport descriptor is issued in practice, or whether any applicant in Greenland has obtained one.

Access to transition-related healthcare in Greenland, and the rules governing gendered facilities such as changing rooms and toilets, are not addressed in the available sources.
